expected_prisoner.name: James W. Douglass
expected_prisoner.description:
Theologian and author ("JFK and the Unspeakable"). Co-founded the Pacific Life Community in January 1975 with his wife Shelley to confront construction of the Trident submarine base at Bangor, WA, after whistleblower Robert Aldridge exposed the system. In November 1977 they purchased 3.8 acres next to the base and named it Ground Zero. Led the White Train tracking campaign and dozens of Bangor line-crossing arrests through the 1980s.

In 1972, while teaching religion at the University of Hawaii, Douglass participated in catholic Action of Hawaii’s Lenten campaign against the air war in Southeast Asia. At Hickam Air Force Base on March 2 he poured blood on military files. The ensuing Hickam Three prosecution ended in misdemeanor convictions, probation and a fine. He later described the action as an attempt to expose the human consequences of electronic warfare. Sources: https://thestreetspirit.org/2015/06/08/street-spirit-interview-with-james-douglass/ ; https://www.ilind.net/2019/07/01/nuremberg-prosecutor-featured-on-60-minutes-defended-hawaii-peace-activists-in-1972-case/ ; https://kyouyou.agu.ac.jp/achievements/file/Journal_204.pdf#page=48
expected_prisoner.body:
Distinct anti-nuclear custody episodes

In his June 8, 2015 Street Spirit interview, Part 2, Douglass describes the August 12, 1982 boat-blockade arrest and detention in a temporary camp near the Trident base. Charges were dropped within days; no exact discharge is stated. This sourced episode now has its own row. The previous generic February 15, 1983 arrest/admission claim was not corroborated and is retained here only as a withdrawn claim, not an exact custody fact.

The same interview separately describes a six-month Boron prison term following the October 28, 1979 mass action. Interviewer Terry Messman's July 1981 release is his own, not a documented release date for Douglass. No endpoint is transferred between the two men or between these separate episodes. Original interview.

expected_cases.sentence: Other anti-nuclear civil-disobedience episodes: exact endpoints remain unverified. The former February 15, 1983 arrest/admission and generic mostly-dismissed/cite-and-release statements were not corroborated by the reviewed primary sources and are withdrawn as structured facts. The separately documented August 12, 1982 boat-blockade detention is recorded in its own row.

expected_cases.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of government property — March 2, 1972 Hickam Three action
expected_cases.sentence: March 2, 1972 action at Hickam Air Force Base; FBI arrest followed on March 8. Convicted of misdemeanor conspiracy and destruction of government property. Received one year of probation and a $500 fine. Initial custody duration is not established. After leaving for Canada and refusing the fine, he was arrested again in 1975 and received two and a half years of probation; probation is not imprisonment. Sources: https://www.ilind.net/2019/07/01/nuremberg-prosecutor-featured-on-60-minutes-defended-hawaii-peace-activists-in-1972-case/ ; https://kyouyou.agu.ac.jp/achievements/file/Journal_204.pdf#page=35 ; https://kyouyou.agu.ac.jp/achievements/file/Journal_204.pdf#page=46

expected_cases.charges: August 12, 1982 Trident peace boat blockade: temporary detention and subsequently dropped felony charges
expected_cases.sentence: Douglass's own interview describes pre-emptive arrest and detention in a temporary camp by the Trident base on August 12, 1982. Felony charges were dropped within a few days, but that does not establish the actual discharge day. This temporary stay is not combined with his earlier Boron prison term or later White Train arrests.
